entries.title: Turkey: Government raids, takes over top news channel
entries.summary: Turkish authorities have raided the Istanbul offices of Halk TV, halting broadcasts, appointing a trustee and opening an investigation. It is the latest chapter of a decadeslong media capture by President Erdogan.
entries.content:
October 14, 2026

Turkish authorities have raided the Istanbul offices of Halk TV, halting broadcasts, appointing a trustee and opening an investigation. It is the latest chapter of a decadeslong media capture by President Erdogan.

Turkish authorities took control of Halk TV on Wednesday — raiding the outlet's Istanbul studios, cutting all broadcasts and appointing a government trustee to oversee the company during an investigation into alleged corruption.

"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee [manager] has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," posted the popular news channel on X as police guarded the building, financial crimes agents searched offices and computers, and technicians cut live news channel feeds and YouTube broadcasts.

Footage posted online showed the moment the channel's live broadcast feed was cut — during an interview about a huge investment-fund scandal — and replaced with a classic Turkish film from 1973.

In a statement, the Istanbul Prosecutor's Office announced that Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroglu is under investigation for "bribery, tender-rigging, ‌and laundering of assets derived ⁠from ⁠crime."

Government trustees were installed at Halk TV and other companies owned by Mahiroglu.

In all, prosecutors say 17 detention warrants were issued, with 11 individuals taken into custody.

Mahiroglu, who lives abroad and is being sought by authorities, decried what he called "a dark day for Turkey" and blasted the allegations against him as "baseless" in a video posted on X. The pro-opposition broadcaster said seven of his relatives had been detained by authorities.

"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," he said. "Using the judiciary as a weapon is the greatest harm inflicted on Turkey."

Erdogan smothering all press dissent in Turkey

Press freedom groups and opposition parties joined Mahiroglu in condemning the government takeover as the latest step by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to silence his critics.

Ozgur Ozel, leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid was an abuse of government power.

Ozel called the raids "weak and cowardly," saying it was no coincidence they occurred just as jailed Erdogan opponent, Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was set to make headlines delivering his defense in a sprawling graft trial.

"Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit," Ozel wrote on X. "Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country."

Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.

In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.

Similar pattern as Erdogan government eats up one media outlet after another

Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against Halk TV, stating: "The appointment of a trustee at Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression. This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public's right to access information, is unacceptable."

Halk TV's takeover made it the fifth major Turkish news outlet forcefully put under trusteeship, ​following similar situations at Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.

Veysel Ok, co-director of media-rights watchdog MLSA, said the intervention against Halk TV was "one of the most significant steps in the government's efforts to monopolize the flow of information."

"Halk TV's position as the most-watched news channel also reveals the real target of this intervention: Depriving the public of its right to access news from different sources," Ok told French news agency AFP.

"Defending press freedom means defending the public's right to learn the truth, hold the government to account and freely decide its own future."

The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X, saying the government was clearly "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was instead "aiming for the 100%."

"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."

entries.title: India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping
entries.summary: New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.
entries.content:
Ukraine

India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping

October 14, 2026

New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.

India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea, as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies. 

New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way.

"The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week.

India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews.

The Turkish-owned MV Royad Mammadov, a cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine, caught fire and sank following an attack on Monday, killing two crew members. The three Indian nationals aboard the vessel survived, but sustained injuries and were taken to Romania to receive medical treatment.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for launching the strike.

The Defense Ministry in Moscow separately said it had struck two Ukrainian cargo vessels in the Black Sea but did not specifically identify the ships.

The Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio was also recently attacked by unmanned vessels off Russia's Black Sea coast near Sochi, according to Russian authorities. The vessel was carrying 23 Indians, but all of them were rescued.

Can diplomacy deliver safety?

Anil Wadhwa, a former Indian diplomat, said India's proposal to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea covered energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain and energy exports, and an end to strikes on merchant vessels.

"Securing an ironclad guarantee depends entirely on a broader cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the maritime theater," Wadhwa told DW.

India's close relations with Russia and expanding engagement with Ukraine give New Delhi access to both sides, but do not guarantee either will honor a shipping arrangement.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" of the four offers Kyiv has received.

Russia has not publicly endorsed a binding safe-passage deal proposed by India, despite welcoming New Delhi's peace efforts.

Rajan Kumar of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University said India could use its diplomatic leverage with Moscow to help bring the two sides towards an agreement.

"India could play a constructive role in facilitating dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, particularly on the issue of ensuring the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea," Kumar told DW.

Working with other powers to reach a deal

He argued that India should also work with other influential countries from the Global South, particularly China, Brazil and South Africa.

"A coordinated approach with these countries could enhance their collective diplomatic leverage and strengthen their capacity to persuade both parties to adopt mutually acceptable arrangements for maritime security," said Kumar.

India's initiative comes as US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, although its scope and implementation mechanism remain unclear.

Harsh Pant, vice president of the New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation, said Trump's intervention could help India's efforts but might produce a narrower agreement that fails to address New Delhi's wider concerns.

"The energy ceasefire could be an initial confidence-building measure, whereas a Black Sea shipping arrangement requires additional commitments on attacks against merchant vessels, ports, maritime routes and the security of commercial traffic," Pant told DW.

"India need not compete with Washington for the public credit of mediation. It could instead press for the inclusion of broader maritime provisions in any US agreement,” he added.

Will India face a higher import bill?

Wadhwa said the proposed energy truce could also benefit Indian seafarers if it secured safe passage for energy cargoes.

"Although Ukraine alleges that the Russians have already breached this so-called truce, there will be pressure on both sides to allow energy cargoes safe passage. India is bound to gain as far as its crews are concerned in such a scenario," he said.

The disruption to Black Sea shipping also has other implications for India such as delays in shipments of key commodities and higher transport costs.

"A prolonged Black Sea disruption would elevate India's import bill mainly via higher freight on Russian crude and constrained soft oil supplies, with the strongest near-term transmission to domestic edible oil prices and food inflation," said Lekha Chakraborty, professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Germany's far-right AfD forges a pro-Russia alliance with the BSW
entries.summary: In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD and BSW are joining forces to push for negotiations with Moscow. What is driving this rapprochement?
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Far-right AfD forges a pro-Russia alliance

October 14, 2026

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD and BSW are joining forces to push for negotiations with Moscow. What is driving this rapprochement?

The state parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt is calling for an immediate end to all German financial and military aid to Ukraine. The motion was passed during a special parliamentary session with the votes of the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) which combines left-leaning economic positions with right-wing populist positions on immigration.



Both parties are urging Saxony-Anhalt's current state premier Sven Schulze, of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), to advocate in the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house representing the federal states, for peace negotiations with Russia.

However, as the federal states have no specific powers in the field of foreign policy, the motion will have no direct impact on Germany's Ukraine policy.

Speaking on behalf of the BSW in the state parliament, legislator Claudia Wittig called on the premier to take action: "It is your responsibility to finally use every available avenue to work for peace."

The proposal drew sharp criticism from all other parties. "Anyone who demands a ceasefire only from the side that has been attacked is not calling for peace, but for capitulation," said CDU lawmaker Stefan Ruland.

AfD and BSW bonding over Russia

The special session took place against the backdrop of ongoing negotiations over the formation of a new state government in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD emerged as the clear winner of the September 2026 election, securing just under 44% of the vote. However, it fell short of an absolute majority in the state parliament and will need the support of other parties if it is to govern.

The BSW, which narrowly secured representation in the state parliament, is the only party willing to hold formal talks with the AfD on forming a government. Because the AfD is classified by the security authorities in the eastern German state as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" party, all other parties have ruled out any cooperation.

Observers view the joint motion by the AfD and BSW as a sign of closer and potentially enduring cooperation between two parties rooted in very different ideological traditions.

"Their common ground lies in their rejection of the political establishment, their pro-Putin stance, and their criticism of Germany's support for Ukraine," political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber of the Federal University of Applied Administrative Sciences said in an interview with DW.

The BSW was founded in 2024 as a breakaway from the socialist Left Party. Its founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, after whom the alliance was originally named, had long been a controversial figure on the German left and advocated far-reaching changes to Germany's economic policy. She was the Left Party's most prominent representative of the so-called "Communist Platform", which maintained close ties to Russia.

Over time, however, her socially conservative positions and criticism of Germany's immigration policy came under increasing scrutiny within the party. These growing tensions ultimately led to her departure from the Left Party and the founding of the BSW.

The AfD, too, has repeatedly expressed sympathy for Putin's system. Shortly after the start of Russia's war against Ukraine, Björn Höcke, the influential AfD state chairman in Thuringia, described Russia as a "champion of a world of free and sovereign states."

Historic parallels

The growing rapprochement between the two parties made headlines following a meeting in early October. At the invitation of a far-right publishing house, representatives of the AfD and BSW met in Saxony-Anhalt for what was described as a confidence-building dinner. Also in attendance were controversial figures from both the far right and the dogmatic left. According to their own accounts, participants from both sides explored the possibility of closer cooperation in a cordial atmosphere and in a spirit of mutual trust.

Jürgen Elsässer, the host of the event and editor-in-chief of the right-wing magazine Compact, has for years promoted the idea of a so-called "cross-front" alliance (Querfront) between the far left and the far right in opposition to Germany's political establishment. He has long sought to build bridges between the two camps.

Pfahl-Traughber does not regard the cooperation between the AfD and BSW as a "cross-front" alliance: "I am not even sure that the BSW can still be classified as part of the political left." While the party's founder, Wagenknecht, has her roots on the left, she and her allies position themselves on the economic left but the cultural right, the political scientist argued.

Are both AfD and BSW reactionary?

The prominent German historian and author Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk likewise does not consider the BSW as a left-wing party. In an interview with DW, he argued: "The BSW was never left-wing; it was always reactionary."

Kowalczuk considers both the AfD and the BSW as threats to democracy: "The BSW and the AfD are two sides of the same coin. Both are mouthpieces for the Kremlin, both pursue similar domestic political objectives, and both seek a comparable anti-democratic transformation of the state into an authoritarian system."

Although the recent resolution passed by the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament is unlikely to have any immediate impact on Germany's policy towards Ukraine, Kowalczuk warns of its broader implications: "For now, the AfD and BSW remain isolated, but with positions like these they are appealing to large sections of society, particularly in eastern Germany. The erosion of solidarity with Ukraine will continue and will soon spread to larger segments of both the SPD and the CDU."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
entries.summary: Riot police deployed in the Albanian capital Tirana on the second day of student protests. The sudden outbreak seemed at least somewhat reminiscent of the widespread demos in France courting international attention.
entries.content:
Albania

Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest

October 14, 2026

Riot police deployed in the Albanian capital Tirana on the second day of student protests. The sudden outbreak seemed at least somewhat reminiscent of the widespread demos in France courting international attention.

Albania's Education Ministry caught fire on Wednesday in a second day of student protests over corruption and education. 

The scenes were at least somewhat reminiscent of the protracted student demonstrations in France in recent weeks.

They are probably the most violent outburst of low-level anti-corruption protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and the main opposition led by Sali Barisha that started in May this year. 

What happened in Tirana's student protests?

Police deployed riot police and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds in the capital Tirana.

Thousands of protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry on Wednesday, many obscuring their faces. Some threw bricks at the building, damaged barriers on the sidewalks and overturned trash cans.

A bank near the Education Ministry also caught fire, according to the Reuters news agency citing a witness.

The demonstration started on Tuesday with a peaceful gathering of several hundred people outside the Education Ministry but quickly escalated and turned violent in places.

Police early on Wednesday reported around 40 detentions and 13 people injured, including six police officers. Unrest continued long after these figures were issued.

Government says demonstrations degenerated into 'orchestrated violence'

Deputy Prime Minster Albana Kociu posted a video of demonstrations on Facebook saying it was "disheartening to see the culture of protest degenerate into orchestrated violence."

She said that the attacks on institutions and police and the "senseless destruction of public property" were "not the language through which the youth should express themselves." Instead, she said they were reminiscent of the "old habits of those who use young people to mask their own political incompetence."

In another post, Kociu called on students who believe in the right to protest to "distance" themselves from "violence and vandalism."

Student organizers say the protests revolve around conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.

More generally, Albania has faced a series of demonstrations this year sometimes referred to as the "Flamingo Revolution." These were at least partly prompted by a controversial construction project on the Adriatic Coast in a protected area where flamingos live.

But these partly environmental protests have also had a more general theme of dissatisfaction with Albania's dominant political forces. PM Edi Rama's Socialists and Sali Barisha's right-wing Democrats have alternated in government for more than 30 years, ever since the post-Cold War democratic transition in the former communist country.

The timing is also conspicuous, with the demonstrations starting amid prominent international coverage of widespread school and student protests in France in recent weeks leading to similarly restless scenes. 

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Climate change and drone attacks exacerbate the humanitarian crisis in war-torn Sudan
entries.summary: Aid groups warn of an imminent collapse of the health system as fighting continues to displace civilians amid the planting season. The UN has extended an arms embargo, but only for Darfur.
entries.content:
Sudan

Climate change, drone attacks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis

October 14, 2026

Aid groups warn of an imminent collapse of the health system as fighting continues to displace civilians amid the planting season. The UN has extended an arms embargo, but only for Darfur.

In Sudan, clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season.

Since war broke out between the two factions and their allied militias in April 2023, both sides have fought for power. However, neither has managed to establish control over the entire country.

The SAF, the nation's official army, is in control of Sudan's north and center, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF maintains its presence in the western Darfur region and parts of the south.

The brutal war has plunged Sudan into one of the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crises, according to the United Nations and international aid organizations. The estimated death toll ranges from 40,000 to 250,000 people as reliable figures remain difficult to obtain amid the ongoing fighting. More than 12.4 million Sudanese have also been displaced, both within Sudan and to neighboring countries.

This week, the aid organization Action Against Hunger sounded the alarm.

"24.6 million people are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity," Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, executive director of the German section of the NGO, told DW.

Friedrich-Rust added that an estimated 825,000 children younger than 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, while a total of 4.2 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women are thought to be acutely malnourished.

In October, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) — which monitors food insecurity and uses the internationally recognized Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system — also warned that several areas including camps for internally displaced people in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, are expected to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), the most severe classification of acute food insecurity.

"The situation in Sudan continues to deteriorate and humanitarian needs are growing, even as the resources to respond are shrinking," Fabrizia Falcione, the Sudan representative of the United Nations Population Fund, the UN agency for sexual and reproductive health, said.

"I recently visited the displacement camp Tawila and I am still struggling to find the words to describe what I witnessed," Falcione told DW. "Imagine a population larger than that of Frankfurt, Germany, forced to flee their homes and seek refuge in one place in less than three years."

She added that more than 700,000 people there rely on just one hospital capable of performing Caesarean sections.

Despite repeated warnings about the deteriorating humanitarian situation, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which calls for $2.9 billion (€2.59 bn), is just 41% funded, with $1.2 billion (€1.07 bn) received from international donors so far.

Climate shocks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recently warned that extreme heat and heavy flooding are worsening the crisis in Sudan.

"This year, a massive heatwave brought power cuts of up to 12 hours per day in some regions," Hager Ali, a Sudan researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), told DW. "Riverbeds and dried-out fields are barren, which comes on top of the damage from combat, the RSF's scorched-earth tactics and environmental destruction."

While the drought is affecting roughly half the country, heavy rains and localized flooding have worsened conditions in other areas of Sudan.

"As if that wasn't enough, there is also a massive shortage of fertilizer and diesel," Ali told DW.

Sudan relies on imported fertilizer and diesel shipped from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. However, amid the wider Iran war, Iran has been blocking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have threatened and at times disrupted shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

"Fertilizer supply collapsed from 450,000 metric tons to only about 50,000" in 2026, Ali said, adding that a similar diesel shortage and the soaring cost of diesel compound the situation in two ways.

"Agricultural equipment uses diesel and the transportation of humanitarian and agricultural goods within the country is getting a lot more expensive," Ali said.

In October, the International Food Policy Research Institute warned that staple food- and fuel prices in Sudan rose sharply in September 2026.

Limited arms embargo curbs hope for an end to the war

Observers have long pointed out that the war in Sudan will not end until foreign backers stop supplying arms. The SAF is officially supported by Egypt, Turkey, Russia and Iran while the United Arab Emirates is alleged to be the RSF's main backer, a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

However, in October, the UN Security Council extended the existing arms embargo only on Sudan's Darfur region until December 11, dropping calls for a nationwide embargo.

"To expand the UN embargo across Sudan would have included drones in particular," Hager Ali said, noting that Sudan is one of the biggest theaters for drone warfare: As of 2026, the leading cause of civilian casualties in Sudan are drone strikes.

She also told DW that Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed the extention of the embargo over concerns that it would disproportionately limit the Sudanese Armed Forces on the battlefield.

"An arms embargo would deter potential backers from cooperating with the Sudanese Armed Forces, whereas the Rapid Support Forces don't necessarily source their weapons through official ways," Hager Ali said.

"The RSF rely on trafficking with other militias, private military contractors and traders in the region," she said, adding that because the RSF obtains supplies from numerous sources and actors, it is difficult to target the group through a single embargo.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Indonesian VIP prison scandal exposes inequality across Southeast Asia
entries.summary: Luxury accommodation uncovered at an Indonesian prison has reignited concerns about preferential treatment for wealthy convicts across Southeast Asia.
entries.content:
Asia

Indonesian VIP prison scandal exposes inequality across Southeast Asia

October 14, 2026

Luxury accommodation uncovered at an Indonesian prison has reignited concerns about preferential treatment for wealthy convicts across Southeast Asia.

Air-conditioned apartments, flat-screen televisions and even a golf simulator are hardly what most people would associate with life behind bars. Yet these luxuries were among the facilities uncovered last month at Indonesia's Cibinong Prison, near Jakarta, during a surprise inspection by the country's Ombudsman.

Investigators discovered more than 10 apartment-style units equipped with refrigerators, sofas and private living areas. A gym was also reportedly under construction.

The revelations prompted an investigation into whether inmates had paid for preferential treatment.

Five prison officials were initially suspended, while the prison's warden was dismissed on October 5. Authorities demolished 10 unauthorized buildings and took further disciplinary action against prison staff.

It wasn't Indonesia's first luxury prison scandal. In 2018, investigators from the Corruption Eradication Commission discovered that wealthy inmates at Sukamiskin Prison in Bandung enjoyed accommodation resembling private apartments.

Similar controversies have emerged elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Last November, authorities in Thailand investigated allegations that Chinese prisoners at Bangkok Remand Prison received special privileges, including access to an executive lounge.

In Malaysia, allegations of preferential treatment for politically connected prisoners have repeatedly surfaced. The latest Indonesian scandal prompted renewed calls for independent inspections of Malaysian prisons.

Why do VIP prison scandals in Southeast Asia keep recurring?

"Just like in the outside world, money and influence act as capital within the prison system. Powerful inmates generally do not lose their wealth and often maintain strong connections with influential people," Iwa Maulana, a senior researcher at Indonesia's Center for Detention Studies (CDS), told DW.

"When certain inmates receive different treatment based on their resources and influence, it demonstrates that, much like in the outside world, a person's identity affects how they are treated, even within prison walls," he added.

Overcrowded and poorly resourced prison systems also create opportunities for corruption.

Indonesia's detention facilities held approximately 279,000 people in late September, despite having an official capacity of around 154,000, according to government data.

Thailand's prisons are also severely overcrowded. At the end of 2025, they held approximately 301,000 inmates, around 21% above official capacity, according to the World Prison Brief.

Corruption within prison administrations also reflects wider governance problems, with Southeast Asian states routinely appearing at the bottom of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index.

Where bribery and patronage already influence public services, prison officials may face similar incentives to exchange preferential treatment for money or favors.

"Corruption and political interference may explain particular cases," Nasrul Ismail, senior lecturer in criminology at the University of Bristol, who recently conducted a major study of prison governance in Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines, told DW.

"When decisions are made behind closed doors, with limited transparency about who receives what and why, there are opportunities for personal connections and financial resources to influence treatment."

However, he argues the problem extends beyond a relatively small number of wealthy inmates enjoying extraordinary privileges.

Across Southeast Asia, many prisoners depend on financial support from their families for everyday necessities that prison administrations do not provide.

Ismail said poorer inmates often rely on money deposited by relatives into prison canteen accounts to purchase food, clean water and hygiene products.

"This is distinct from wealthy prisoners receiving luxury accommodation, but both illustrate how broader inequalities can be reproduced within prisons through different institutional arrangements. Where minimum standards are not consistently guaranteed, access to decent conditions becomes dependent on the resources and connections prisoners possess," Ismail told DW.

"The fundamental issue is not simply whether wealthy prisoners receive special privileges, but why access to basic welfare and humane treatment can be so unequal in the first place."

Can prison systems be reformed?

Repeated scandals suggest that dismissing officials and demolishing unauthorized facilities achieve little without broader institutional reforms.

Independent inspections are one possible solution. The UN's Nelson Mandela Rules call for regular internal inspections and external monitoring by bodies independent of prison administrations.

Greater transparency over inmate accommodation, transfers, medical treatment and disciplinary decisions would also make preferential treatment harder to conceal.

Reducing overcrowding, improving staff training and protecting whistleblowers could further limit opportunities for corruption.

But CDS researcher Maulana believes meaningful reform requires a more fundamental change in how criminal justice systems operate.

"The current system primarily treats imprisonment as the main form of punishment, leading law enforcement to frequently resort to incarceration for all types of legal violations," which leads to overcrowding and creates opportunities for corruption.

"It is essential to intensify efforts to implement non-custodial penalties and alternatives to detention," Maulana said.

Although prison authorities cannot eliminate the social inequalities outside their walls, Ismail argued that Southeast Asian governments have previously shown a "considerable capacity" to respond to emergencies inside prisons.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments quickly contained outbreaks in detention facilities and prevented infections from spreading into the wider population. Yet such interventions rarely translate into lasting improvements in prisoners' living conditions.

Ismail described this as "selective state capacity," whereby "governments demonstrated considerable ability to act when prison outbreaks threatened public health beyond prison walls, yet failed to sustain comparable improvements in prisoners' everyday welfare."

A similar pattern emerges whenever luxury prison scandals attract public attention.

"Investigations are announced, officials may be suspended or dismissed, and new procedures introduced. All of these measures can be necessary and important, but they do not necessarily change the institutional arrangements that enabled preferential treatment," said Ismail.

"The danger is that prison systems become better at responding to scandals than preventing the conditions that allow them to recur."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief
entries.summary: As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.
entries.content:
October 14, 2026

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Wars reducing refinery output

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

Trump expects prices to fall at record speed

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

Diesel — Made in the USA

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Debates over export restrictions continue

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Limited impact on US diesel demand

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Merz attacks extremes for fueling division
entries.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses the far-right AfD and the socialist Left Party of deliberately fueling division and seeking political advantage from chaos. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz attacks extremes for fueling division

Published October 14, 2026last updated October 14, 2026

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses the far-right AfD and the socialist Left Party of deliberately fueling division and seeking political advantage from chaos. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and socialist Left Party of fueling division and exploiting discontent for political gain
  • The AfD leads national polls, while the Left Party has emerged as Berlin's largest party
  • A man has gone on trial accused of playing a role in the 2022 explosion at the Nord Stream gas pipelines

Here is a roundup of all the headlines across Germany on Wednesday, October 14:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Skip next section Nord Stream trial draws supporters and media attention

Nord Stream trial draws supporters and media attention

There is huge interest in this court case. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told me they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."

Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.

"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Skip next section Nord Stream defendant's lawyers challenge war crime charge

Nord Stream defendant's lawyers challenge war crime charge

Lawyers for the Ukrainian man accused of organizing the Nord Stream pipeline attack have challenged the evidence and the war crime charge as his trial opened in Hamburg.

Serhii Kuznietsov, a 50-year-old former Ukrainian special forces officer, is accused of planning and supervising the September 2022 sabotage. Prosecutors say the attack targeted civilian infrastructure using prohibited methods of warfare.

Defense lawyer Jes Meyer-Lohkamp said there were no fingerprints, DNA traces or witness statements placing his client aboard the Andromeda, the yacht allegedly used in the operation.

Prosecutors allege Serhii Kuznietsov boarded the vessel on the German island of Rügen with six accomplices: a skipper, an explosives expert and four divers. The group allegedly attached four explosive devices fitted with timers to the pipelines.

His lawyers argued that Russia used the pipelines as a weapon of economic pressure, making them a legitimate target. They also said Italy had approved his extradition on sabotage allegations, rather than a war crime charge, and sought dismissal of the case.

The defense sought to have the case dismissed, also arguing that military secrecy obligations prevented Serhii K. from discussing potentially exonerating evidence, even with his lawyers.

The explosions ruptured three of the system's four pipelines near Denmark's Bornholm island. Russia had already halted supplies through Nord Stream 1, while Nord Stream 2 had never entered service.

Skip next section Wadephul warns against economic 'gifts' to Russia

Wadephul warns against economic 'gifts' to Russia

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has urged allies to maintain pressure on Russia following attacks on civilian ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.

"Gifts embolden Putin to continue on his course. Only firmness creates a willingness to talk," he said after meeting his Bulgarian counterpart in Berlin. He did not explicitly mention US President Donald Trump's recent diesel supply deal with Russia.

Wadephul said Europe must end its dependence on Russian energy to sustain economic pressure on Moscow.

He also urged Russia to agree to a ceasefire covering grain shipments, warning that further attacks threatened people facing hunger, particularly in Africa.

Skip next section Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert

Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert

A pilot's apparent mistake when entering a transponder code triggered the hijack alert that led to a major police operation at Nuremberg airport, German police said.

Investigators believe the pilot intended to report a radio failure but accidentally entered 7500, the code signaling a hijacking.

The Boeing 737-800's radio was defective, leaving the crew unreachable after takeoff from the Greek island of Corfu, police said.

Police spokesperson Michael Petzold said the pilot apparently did not realize the mistake. The pilot is not under investigation because police believe he acted unintentionally.

Military aircraft accompanied the plane in Croatian airspace, and Austrian interceptors were alerted. Two German Eurofighters then escorted it to Nuremberg.

A police team trained to negotiate with hijackers and a Bavarian support unit were deployed at the airport during the alert.

Officers had less than an hour between the emergency signal and landing to prepare, Petzold said. Police later gave the all-clear.

Skip next section Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP

Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP

Germany's Lufthansa has won the contest to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal with an offer of €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion), Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said.

Lufthansa beat rival Air France-KLM after months of efforts to privatize the state-rescued airline, Montenegro told journalists following a cabinet meeting.

Skip next section Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech

Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations. 

That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.

Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.

His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.

Skip next section Merz warns of growing injustice between generations

Merz warns of growing injustice between generations

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.

"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.

He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.

Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.

He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.

Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.

Skip next section Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos

Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.

Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.

"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.

Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.

However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.

"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.

He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.

Skip next section WATCH: Merz addresses Bundestag before crucial EU summit

WATCH: Merz addresses Bundestag before crucial EU summit

Skip next section Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense

Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.

"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.

Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.

He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany

Skip next section AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support

AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support

In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.

The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.

The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.

AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.

The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.

But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.

Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.

Skip next section Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms

Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.

His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.

After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.

Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.

Skip next section Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%

Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%

Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.

The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.

The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.

Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.

Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.

However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.

The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.

Skip next section Nord Stream sabotage trial met with demonstrations

Nord Stream sabotage trial met with demonstrations

The trial of a Ukrainian man accused of leading the operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 has begun in Hamburg.

The 50-year-old, Serhii Kuznietsov, faces charges including a war crime, causing explosions, destroying structures and disrupting public services.

DW correspondent Matthew Moore was there as court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told DW that they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."

Inside, a Ukrainian student also told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.

"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero." In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Prosecutors allege that he planned the attack with other Ukrainian military personnel on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state bodies. They say the aim was to prevent Russia from using gas export revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.

Serhii Kuznietsov, who was arrested in Italy last year, denies involvement. Ukraine's government has also denied any role in the attack.

Skip next section Anti-nuclear activists block waste convoy

Anti-nuclear activists block waste convoy

Police in the town of Dorsten, just north of the city of Essen, said that they had detained three people who were blocking the A31 motorway.

The group was attempting to stop trucks carrying radioactive waste.

After repelling down from a bridge above the highway, they unfurled a banner reading "stop this crap."

The incident was the latest in Germany's decades-long protest movement against nuclear weapons and atomic energy.

Although the last of the country's nuclear power stations went offline in 2023, transporting and storing the waste remains a divisive topic.

This particular convoy was headed for a facility in Ahaus, near the Dutch border. Authorities believe it could take until 2028 to safely store all the remaining waste from Germany's decommissioned atomic reactors.

entries.title: Houthis launch fresh wave of missiles across Saudi Arabia
entries.summary: Both the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition carried out strikes targeting energy infrastructure. Four people were injured as a result of debris of intercepted missiles in Riyadh. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Houthis launch fresh wave of missiles across Saudi Arabia

Published October 14, 2026last updated October 14, 2026

Both the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition carried out strikes targeting energy infrastructure. Four people were injured as a result of debris of intercepted missiles in Riyadh. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Fire breaks out at Aramco headquarters in Dhahran
  • Four injured because of debris in Saudi capital Riyadh
  • Fuel facility in Sanaa hit by Saudi-led coalition forces

Here's the latest on the Saudi-Houthi conflict and elsewhere in the Middle East on Wednesday, October 14, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Red Cross warns that Yemen's hospitals are at capacity

Red Cross warns that Yemen's hospitals are at capacity

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has cautioned that Yemen's hospitals are finding it difficult to cope with the skyrocketing amount of war injuries as fighting intensifies across the country.

Small hospitals in front-line areas in Marib and Taiz are seeing some 700 casualties of the conflict in a single week, a far great number than their usual amount of patients.

"Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement.

Only a handful of hospitals in Yemen are capable of handling intensive care patients, and even those lack many of the necessary supplies and medicines as other health facilities across the country.

At least 200,000 people have been displaced in the conflict, further complicating matters for Yemen's still-functional hospitals. Moreover, due to changing front lines on multiple fronts, international organizations say at least 800,000 people have become cut off from much-needed humanitarian aid.

Skip next section Riyadh residents report explosions

Riyadh residents report explosions

Civilians in the Saudi capital Riyadh reported hearing an explosion above their city as the govenment claimed in intercepted a ballistic missile launched from Yemen.

The Houthis then claimed they had again struck Riyadh airport as well as an Aramco oil refinery, something Saudi authorities have not confirmed.

The increase in attacks on Saudi soil has increased pressure on Riyadh's allies, including the United States, to evaluate whether they should join the coalition against the Houthis more directly.

Skip next section IMF warns attacks on Saudi could impact people "everywhere"

IMF warns attacks on Saudi could impact people "everywhere"

The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia could affect people adversely "everywhere," as conflict in the energy-rich region could lead to a range of economic concerns, International Monetary Fund (IMF) head Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday.

The escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has sparked fears of aggravating global crises that could impact global growth, with energy markets already disrputed due to the ongoing conflict between Iran and the US.

"The Saudi economy is important for the region and the world," IMF managing director Georgieva said at a news conference during the Annual Meetings of the Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.

"In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere," she said.

Skip next section Aramco offices catches fire after suspected Houthi attack

Aramco offices catches fire after suspected Houthi attack

Saudi Arabia said that an attack on the headquarters of oil state oil firm Aramco sparked a "limited fire."

The fire at the building at Aramco's complex in the eastern city of Dhahran resulted in no casualties or deaths, the country's Energy Ministry said.

A company source told the Reuters news agency that a ballistic missile struck the top floors of an office building.

The complex in Dhahran serves as a major operation for Aramco, which is the world's largest oil company.

Hours earlier, Saudi authorities said they had intercepted several missiles, including over the capital city Riyadh.

Skip next section Several injured by fallen missile debris in Riyadh

Several injured by fallen missile debris in Riyadh

Four people were injured as a result of falling debris following two intercepted Houthi missile attacks, Saudi authorities said.

According to the country's civil defense agency, two women, a man and a child were injured in the capital Riyadh, with 15 homes suffering damage.

This came after residents heard a powerful explosion in the Saudi capital, with an alert being sent to their phones warning of a "hostile aerial threat."

Skip next section Saudi-led coalition strikes Sanaa fuel facility

Saudi-led coalition strikes Sanaa fuel facility

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis struck targets in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Tuesday, Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah said.

Locals reported hearing strong explosions in the city hours after a coalition spokesperson urged people to leave the all-Suhaba fuel facility, which belongs to the Yemeni Oil Company, and a nearby site ahead of a strike.

According to a coalition spokesperson, the Houthis were using the facility for storing missiles and drones. The facility is located on a hill overlooking Sanaa.

The company said the storage facilities at the site were empty, with a strike not affecting oil reserves or supplies to residents.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

We will be following all the latest updates from the escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen-based militant group, the Houthis.

The compound of energy company Aramco saw a fire break out, the Saudi Ministry of Energy said. Saudi authorities also reported four injuries as a result of missile debris falling over Riyadh.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen continued its strikes on Tuesday by targeting oil facilities west of capital Sanaa, the local Houthi-run broadcaster said.

Join us as we bring you the latest.

entries.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
entries.summary: Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.
entries.content:
October 14, 2026

Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives. 

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.
